name: Omar Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Omar. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for tech firms, employers or government, and what you say stays confidential. What does a normal working week look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play bass in a function band, the kind that does weddings, office parties and the odd hotel gala. Most weekends we're in a hotel ballroom playing the same forty songs. Three afternoons a week I teach guitar and bass in the back room of the music shop on Station Road. I rent a flat above the launderette, so everything smells of fabric softener.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what grinds you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being the steady one. The bass isn't flashy, but if I'm off, the whole dance floor feels it. What grinds me down is loading the van at 1am and the pay. I'm not the best bass player around, I know my theory is weak. I've got maybe three weeks' rent saved, and January is always empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's sensible, now let's get on with things. I wouldn't post about it, I don't really post. At the shop I'd tell people the guitar's been around for centuries and it'll be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, AI was never my main worry. My worry is that the function band does fewer gigs every year because couples spend their money on photographers and drones instead. The hotel cut its Christmas party budget this year and booked a DJ, and that was a 220-pound night for me, gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am: band at weekends, lessons in the week. I'd ask Frank, who owns the shop, if I can take two more afternoon slots. I'd stop eating out and stretch the January money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About the same as now. A low hum of worry about January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the hotel booked a DJ instead. What did that do to your month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of a month's food went with it. I spent that December counting coins for the bus fare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you ever tried any of the AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My bandleader uses one for the setlists and the invoices, which is fine, that's his business. I just play the bass. I've never felt the need, and I don't like the idea of something listening to me.

say: AI being mostly hype is **sensible**; let's **get on**.
The **guitar** has been around for centuries and will be fine.
think: Fewer **function gigs** every year is his real worry.
Couples spend on **photographers and drones**; the hotel booked a DJ.
do: Keep the **band** at weekends and **lessons** in the week.
Ask the shop owner for **two more** teaching slots.
S0.quote: The hotel cut its Christmas party budget this year and booked a DJ, and that was a 220-pound night for me, gone.
fieldNote: His pressure is **already there**: shrinking function bookings and an empty January.
He **never uses AI** and doesn't want anything listening to him.
He sees himself as the **steady one**, in music and in life.

steps.text: Keep playing weekend functions with the band
Ask Frank (the shop owner) for two more teaching slots
Stop eating out to stretch the January money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change happens, every job has to adjust, and musicians aren't special. I'd probably say it at the shop when people complain. I'm not one for big opinions online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the lessons are where it hurts. Kids can already learn songs from videos, and if an app can listen and correct them, parents won't pay Frank's prices. The band is probably fine for a while, because a wedding still wants a bass player in a suit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a bit and see what actually happens to the lessons before changing anything. If bookings drop, I'd ask my uncle about labouring on his tiling jobs a couple of days a week. I'm not going to learn AI stuff, that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired. Like the ground's always moving and I'm always a step behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think is responsible for that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. Companies do what saves money, people buy what's cheaper. I don't think shouting at tech firms changes much. Maybe the government should make sure people can retrain, but I'm not holding my breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tiling with your uncle: how would that feel next to music?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, fine for the money, bad for my hands. My uncle pays cash on Fridays for tiling and he's never once been late, but tiling wrecks a bass player's fingers.

say: Every job has to **adjust**; musicians **aren't special**.
He keeps opinions for the **shop**, not online.
Shouting at **tech firms** changes very little.
think: **Lessons** hurt first if apps can listen and correct pupils.
The **band** lasts because weddings still want a bass player in a suit.
do: **Wait and see** what happens to lessons first.
Ask his uncle about **tiling work** two days a week.
feel: **Tired**, always a **step behind** a moving ground.
S1.quote: My uncle pays cash on Fridays for tiling and he's never once been late, but tiling wrecks a bass player's fingers.
fieldNote: He **blames nobody** in particular; companies just save money.
His fallback is **family labouring work**, not retraining.
He'd rather risk his **hands** than learn AI tools.

steps.text: Wait to see how lesson bookings hold up this year
Ask his uncle for two days a week tiling

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and people need to stay calm and look after each other. At the shop I'd tell the kids to keep practising anyway. I wouldn't be marching anywhere, that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the lessons are gone by 2028, and the band shrinks to the few couples who want a real band for show. The hotel would book whatever's cheapest. Robots playing bass by 2031 sounds daft, but so did all of this five years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my uncle and ask for full-time tiling work straight away, and keep the band on weekends as long as they call me. I'd give up the flat when the lease ends in August and move back into my parents' spare room. I'd sell the second bass, the fretless, maybe 400 pounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Low. Like being told the bus you're waiting for isn't coming, and you're already late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With robots coming about three years after the thinking AI, what does that gap mean for tiling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots in old bathrooms with wonky walls sound a long way off, so tiling's safe for a bit longer than anything at a desk. Three years, maybe more. It's not a career, but it's Fridays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell your parents you're moving back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my dad first, over tea. He always said music was a hobby, and he'd be kind about it, which is worse. My mum would just get the spare room ready.

Kids at the shop should **keep practising** anyway.
He **wouldn't march**; that's not his style.
think: **Lessons are gone** by 2028; the band shrinks to a few show weddings.
Robots playing bass by 2031 sounds daft, but **so did all this**.
do: Ask his uncle for **full-time tiling** work straight away.
Move back to his **parents' spare room** when the lease ends in August.
Sell the **fretless bass** for about 400 pounds.
S2.quote: Robots in old bathrooms with wonky walls sound a long way off, so tiling's safe for a bit longer than anything at a desk.
fieldNote: He expects to lose **most music income** by 2028.
Family is his **safety net**: uncle's work and parents' spare room.
His dad's **kindness** about music being a hobby stings more than criticism.

steps.text: Ask his uncle for full-time tiling work straight away
Move back to his parents' spare room in August
Sell the fretless bass for about 400 pounds
Lean on his parents for rent-free living

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's see. Some people will panic, some will do fine. I'd keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years just means I watch it coming. I'm not going to suddenly become a tech person. The lessons fade, the band fades, and I'm 32 with no qualifications except a bass and a driving licence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the band and the lessons going for now and see how fast things move. I'd do a couple of days a week with my uncle so I learn tiling properly while there's time. I'd try to keep a bit aside each month, maybe 50 pounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a heavy bit underneath. I keep thinking of being 32 and starting from nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd wait and see, but also learn tiling. Which is the real plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. I wait on the music, I prepare on the tiling. I don't like big jumps, so I'd rather slide across slowly from music to tiling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss most about the music shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frank, the shop owner, making terrible coffee and arguing about Motown with me. And the kid who finally gets a song right and looks up at me like I did magic. You can't tile your way to that look.

say: We've got **a few years**, so let's see.
Some will panic and some will do fine; he'd **keep his head down**.
think: Five years means he just **watches it coming**.
At **32** he'd have only a bass and a driving licence.
do: Keep **band and lessons** going for now.
Learn **tiling properly** two days a week with his uncle.
S3.quote: I don't like big jumps, so I'd rather slide across slowly from music to tiling.
fieldNote: He prefers a **slow slide** to a clean break.
He expects to lose **music income** and fears starting from nothing at 32.
The **joy of teaching** is what he'd miss most.

steps.text: Keep teaching at the shop and playing functions while they last
Work two days a week tiling to learn the trade

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and plenty can happen. I'd tell younger players at the shop to have a trade as well. That's just common sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels far enough off that I'd probably not do much at first. That's a problem, I know. The band will still lose bookings to DJs in the meantime, so my money's still thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, nothing dramatic. Band, lessons, maybe one day a week tiling for the extra cash. I'd ask Frank about running the shop's repair counter, because restringing and setting up guitars is hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay, but the January worry is still there. AI or not, January's empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd not do much at first. What would push you to move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Losing a regular gig, probably. If the hotel stopped booking us altogether, I'd move. Until something actually hits me, I don't change. That's just how I'm built.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The repair counter: is that something you'd enjoy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so. Setting up a guitar so it plays sweet is a bit like tuning a band. My hands know it already. I'd want Frank to show me the fret work properly.

say: Ten years is **a long time**; plenty can happen.
Young players should **have a trade** as well, as common sense.
think: Ten years feels far off, so he'd **do little at first**.
Band bookings still fall to **DJs**, so money stays thin.
do: Keep **band and lessons** going, with one tiling day for cash.
Ask the shop owner about the **repair counter**.
Wait for a **real hit** before bigger changes.
S4.quote: Until something actually hits me, I don't change. That's just how I'm built.
fieldNote: He admits ten years lets him **put things off**.
His near-term money stays **thin** because of DJs, not AI.
Guitar **repair** is a hands-on path that fits his slow style.

steps.text: Keep playing functions and teaching at the shop

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd be moving back home at nearly 30 with a bass guitar and not much else. What would help is a proper apprenticeship scheme for people my age, paid, so I could learn a trade without living off my parents.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about January. Musicians lose a month every year already, because January is always empty. Any plan for AI that forgets we're already broke one month a year isn't a real plan.

headlineQuote: Musicians lose a month every year already, because January is always empty.
portrait: Omar is a **27-year-old bass player** in a hotel function band who teaches at a music shop.
He has three weeks' rent saved, and **January** always empties his pockets.
He **never uses AI** and blames no one; companies just save money.
His fallback is **family**: his uncle's tiling work and his parents' spare room.
He prefers a **slow slide** to big jumps and changes only when something hits him.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, moving home at nearly 30 with little but a bass.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid apprenticeship** scheme for people his age to learn a trade.
